From Washington on 20 July 1861, William H. Seward sent orders to Carl Schurz in Madrid. The letter is document 171 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote to Madrid on the eve of Bull Run, in the last hours of the short war mood. His orders to Schurz share the bold tone of that week. The letter stands in the file just before defeat abroad and at home reshaped every plan. News of Bull Run would reach Madrid within days and test Schurz's fresh standing. Fresh standing at a proud court is a frail thing after news of defeat.
frus-1861-d271:
Word from Mr. Brown reached Washington on 11 June 1861, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 271 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d71:
On 26 May 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 71 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d171:
Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams in London on 27 October 1862, and the letter stands as Document 171 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It came near the end of a busy month of Atlantic mail.

Late October brought word that France wanted Britain and Russia to join it in urging a truce on the warring Americans. Washington opposed any such step, which would treat the South as a power in its own right. Seward's letters of this period, this one among them, kept his London envoy ready for the talks ahead. Cotton hunger in British mill towns kept the war a kitchen-table topic across the North of England.
frus-1862-d271:
Dated 28 April 1862, Document 271 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume among the French papers.

By the time this letter reached Paris, New Orleans was in Union hands and the fact was known in Europe. Seward's mail in the following weeks pressed the lesson that the South was shrinking. Dayton used such letters in his calls at the foreign ministry, where France's leaders still kept their options open on the war. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d371:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward answered Viscount Treilhard on 9 August 1862, a day after Treilhard's first letter in this file. The reply is Document 371 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

A next-day answer marks a channel working in the same city at walking pace, unlike the slow Atlantic mails. Treilhard's letters and Seward's replies alternate through the late summer of 1862. Together they show two offices in Washington dealing promptly, in writing, while the war's outcome hung in doubt after a season of Union defeats. Formal calls between the two men were frequent, and their notes followed up the talks.
frus-1862-d471:
On 20 October 1862 George Perkins Marsh reported from Turin to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 471 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

Marsh wrote a month after Antietam, as the emancipation order's meaning sank in across Europe. In Italy, where the war was read through the lens of national unity, the news strengthened the Union's moral standing. His October report measured that shift for Washington. Marsh's Turin letters, calm and observant, give the reader a southern-European vantage on the war. That vantage lies far from the London and Paris exchanges. Those exchanges dominate most accounts of Civil War diplomacy.
frus-1862-d571:
Henry Shelton Sanford received the year's closing Belgian order from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 19 November 1862. It is Document 571 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

November 1862 brought France's mediation proposal and the Union's flat refusal, which Seward communicated to every post. Sanford in Brussels, with his court's lines into London, was a useful place to have the refusal understood. The instruction ends a year of unusually brisk dealing between Washington and its Belgian legation. Judged by the file's density, the small post had earned its keep. Information came in and instructions went out. A friendly court stayed friendly through the war's hardest year so far.
frus-1862-d671:
Writing on 23 January 1862, Anson Burlingame sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Burlingame was the American minister to China, in the first year of his mission. The dispatch appears as document 671 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Burlingame wrote as a man who liked China and meant to deal fairly with its court, a stance that later made him famous. His early letters set out what he saw and what he thought the United States should do. This dispatch belongs to that first season, when the new envoy was still learning the ground and telling Washington what he found.
frus-1863p1-d71:
This second letter of 3 February 1863 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 71 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, paired with the letter printed just before it.

Short, split letters were Seward's way of keeping a brief in order. Adams could act on each sheet as its matter came up in his talks with Lord Russell. This one is the second half of the day's work from Washington. It belongs to the steady stream by which the Union held its ground in Britain through the war's hardest winter.
frus-1863p1-d171:
On 24 April 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 171 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second of Seward's sheets held its own head of the brief, as the file's pairs always did. With Adams's three letters of the same date, the day's pile in the volume runs to five. This letter is Washington's last word in that pile. It closes the peak day of late April, a small monument to how much of the war was waged in ink.
frus-1863p1-d271:
Frederick W. Seward, the Assistant Secretary of State and the Secretary's son, wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 22 August 1863. His letter is document 271 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

When the Secretary was away or overloaded, his son and deputy signed the department's letters. The London instructions therefore sometimes ran under the younger Seward's hand, though the policy stayed the Secretary's. The chief aim was unchanged: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Orders crossed by steamship, and Adams had to act on them in talks with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary.
frus-1863p1-d371:
Britain's side of the Washington exchange speaks in this note, sent by Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 January 1863. It is document 371 of the 1863 papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Under the formal courtesy sits real tension: a neutral Britain trading with both sides, and a Union government sure that trade kept the South alive. This exchange is where the two views met. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d471:
On 22 April 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d571:
Under the date 17 June 1863, the record holds a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d671:
Document 671, dated 20 November 1863, records a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late autumn of 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

Each crossing of the Atlantic took the better part of two weeks, so these letters also show leaders acting on news that was already old. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
plos-pbio-0020171:
Alexander Kohlmaier, Fabio Savarese, Monika Lachner, and their team studied X chromosome shutdown in PLOS Biology in 2004. Female cells carry two X chromosomes but use only one. A gene called Xist starts the shutdown, and chemical marks on histones spread the silent state.

The authors found that Xist leaves a kind of memory on the chromosome. That memory guides where the silencing marks land as shutdown proceeds. The idea of a stored mark helps explain how a brief signal creates a lasting state. X inactivation is a model for all long term gene silencing, so its rules inform work on development and disease far beyond this one chromosome.
plos-pbio-0020271:
Mark D. Schroeder, Michael Pearce, John Fak, and co-workers mapped gene control in the fly embryo in PLOS Biology in 2004. A network of segmentation genes cuts the early embryo into repeating bands, the first step toward body segments. Switches that turn these genes on and off set the band edges.

The team charted those switches across the genome and tied them to the genes they control. A full wiring chart shows how a handful of signals create a precise pattern from a smooth start. That precision from loose beginnings is a core wonder of development. The fly network remains one of the best worked examples of it, used to teach and to test new ideas.
plos-pone-0000071:
Nicola Franscini, Ahmed El Gedaily, Ulrich Mahlfeld, and their team tested milk for prion protein in PLOS ONE in 2006. Prions cause BSE in cattle and related brain diseases. The normal form of the prion protein sits in many tissues, and the question was whether it appears in milk from healthy animals.

Finding the normal protein in milk does not mean milk spreads disease; the harmful folded form is the danger. Still, knowing where the normal form occurs guides safety testing. Dairy products reach nearly everyone, so even small risks deserve careful checks. The study gives food safety science a firm fact to build on, replacing guesswork about one common food.
plos-pone-0000171:
Angeline Rose Babel, James Bruce, and John A. T. Young published this virology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies the envelope glycoprotein of subgroup B avian sarcoma and leukosis virus, a bird virus. Two parts of that outer protein, the hr1 region and the fusion peptide, are examined for their role in fusing membranes at low pH.

A virus must merge its envelope with a cell to get inside, and acidity is the trigger here. The authors pinpoint how the two regions shape that fusion step. The details matter for understanding retrovirus entry in general, including how better-studied human viruses breach cells.
plos-pone-0000271:
Tim van Opijnen, Anthony de Ronde, Maarten C. Boerlijst, and colleagues published this HIV evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Its finding is in the title: how HIV-1 adapts depends on the host-cell environment it grows in. The same virus, placed in different cell types, evolves along different paths.

That dependence matters because HIV lives in several kinds of cells in the body. A drug or immune pressure that works in one cell type may select different escape routes in another. The paper warns that lab studies in a single cell line can misread how the virus will evolve in a patient.
plos-pone-0000371:
Taketoshi Kiya, Takekazu Kunieda, and Takeo Kubo studied the honeybee brain in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Forager bees, the workers that leave the hive to gather food, behave very differently from bees that stay inside. The team asked whether a specific group of brain cells works harder in foragers.

The cells sit in the mushroom body, a brain region tied to learning and memory in insects. The authors report increased neural activity in one subtype of these cells in forager brains. Linking a cell group to a bee's job in the colony helps explain how brains support the division of labor in social insects.
plos-pone-0000471:
Gul Shad Ali and colleagues described a new splicing factor that steers plant development, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Splicing is the editing of a gene's message, cutting out some sections and joining others, which lets one gene make several proteins. The team characterized a novel factor that regulates this editing in plants.

Developmental processes from flowering to root growth depend on the right message edits at the right time. A new regulator of splicing adds a control knob biologists did not know plants had. Studies in model plants often transfer to crops, where controlling development can mean better yield or hardiness.
plos-pone-0000571:
Christian E. Badr and colleagues built a sensitive test for a cell's internal shipping stress, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. The secretory pathway moves proteins out of the cell, and the endoplasmic reticulum, where it starts, suffers stress when overloaded. Their highly sensitive assay monitors both the pathway and ER stress.

ER stress is implicated in diabetes, neurodegeneration, and viral infection, so a better gauge has wide use. Sensitivity matters because early, mild stress is when intervention could help most. Assay papers are the plumbing of science: unglamorous, but everything downstream depends on their quality.
plos-pone-0000671:
Koushirou Suga, David Mark Welch, Yukari Tanaka and colleagues catalogued gene tags from a tiny water animal in PLOS ONE in 2007. Rotifers are among the most common non-arthropod animals, and the easiest to work with in their ancient animal group, the Gnathifera. Brachionus plicatilis was becoming a model for ecotoxicology and aquatic ecology.

The team analyzed expressed sequence tags, short reads from active genes, from this rotifer. It reproduces in cycles of parthenogenesis, where females produce offspring without fertilization. A tag catalogue gives researchers handles on its genes for pollution testing and ecology. It also supports studies of its unusual reproductive cycle, which alternates asexual phases with sexual ones.
plos-pone-0000771:
Yixuan Ku, Shinji Ohara, Liping Wang and colleagues traced touch-and-vision links between two brain areas, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their earlier work used event-related potentials recorded from the scalp. One scalp signal, called N140, is evoked by touch vibration in working memory tasks. It grew stronger when subjects expected a visual stimulus that had been paired with the touch. Expectation alone changed the touch response.

Using independent component analysis of the recordings, the team implicated the prefrontal cortex and somatosensory cortex in this crossmodal association. Crossmodal means across senses. The findings help explain how the brain binds touch to sight in memory, a binding everyday life relies on constantly.
plos-pone-0000871:
Ernest Greene studied how the retina handles very brief shape cues, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Shape can be probed by flashing dots along an outline one after another. Gaps of less than a thousandth of a second between dots can already hurt recognition, which raises a puzzle about where the loss happens.

Greene asks whether the eye itself keeps the signal in order, or whether later brain stages do that work. The question goes to how vision turns a stream of flashes into a steady form. It also matters for displays and tests that rely on rapid images. The study keeps the focus on the first stage of seeing.
plos-pone-0000971:
Marie-Christine Desy and Hugo Theoret measured how watching a hand action stirs the viewer's motor cortex, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Watching hand actions raises activity in the observer's own movement system, a response tied to mirror neurons. The brain seems to rehearse what it sees.

The pair asked whether physical similarity between the viewer and the observed hand changes that response. If the mirror system cares about likeness, its firing should shift with how closely the hand matches one's own. Answers shape theories of imitation and empathy. They also matter for rehab methods that use action watching to retrain movement.
plos-pone-0001071:
Elena Gonzalez-Rey, Ruben Martinez-Romero, Francisco O'Valle and colleagues tested a DNA repair enzyme blocker against arthritis, in PLOS ONE in 2007. PARP-1 is an enzyme that helps repair DNA and keep the genome intact. It also drives inflammation forward, and blocking it has eased inflammatory responses in other settings.

The team report a therapeutic effect of a PARP-1 inhibitor on experimental arthritis, by downregulating inflammation and the Th1 immune response. One target touching both joint inflammation and the immune pattern behind it is attractive. Arthritis drugs often trade benefit for broad immune suppression, so any narrower route deserves the test this paper gives.
plos-pone-0001171:
Mosquito bites do more than deliver viruses; the insect's saliva changes the skin it enters. Bradley Schneider and colleagues asked whether past contact with uninfected mosquitoes affects later West Nile virus infection, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. West Nile virus is inoculated in vector saliva into the skin and circulation of its hosts.

The authors report that prior exposure to uninfected mosquitoes enhanced mortality in naturally transmitted West Nile virus infection. The result is counterintuitive, since exposure might be expected to protect. It suggests that immune memory of mosquito saliva can worsen a later viral infection, a factor vaccine designers may need to consider.
plos-pone-0001271:
Clostridium botulinum makes the botulinum neurotoxins, among the most potent poisons known, causing long-lasting and potentially fatal intoxication. Theresa Smith and colleagues analyzed the genes for the toxin complex in several strains, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Toxin variants are grouped into types by their amino acid differences.

The authors report where several toxin gene clusters sit in the A1-A4 and B1 strains examined. Clusters including BoNT/A3, /Ba4, and /B1 are located within plasmids, the small DNA circles bacteria trade between themselves. Mobile toxin genes raise questions about how new toxin types arise and spread.
plos-pone-0001371:
Anne Charlotte Grüner and co-authors published a 2007 PLOS ONE study on malaria shots. Most shots aim to build a strong response to one key part of a germ. That plan has worked well for germs and viruses, but not yet for the parasites that cause malaria. The team tested what drives full, sterile defense in their model.

The authors found that this full defense did not rest on the response to the main surface protein of the parasite. That was a surprise, since that protein had been a top shot target for years. The result pushes shot makers to look past one protein. It suggests broad defense may need a wider set of targets.
plos-pone-0001471:
Cheikh Sokhna and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on guarding children from malaria in Senegal. In the Sahel, most malaria deaths hit children aged one to four in a short wet season. An past trial of seasonal preventive drugs cut cases by a large share. This trial tested four drug plans head to head.

The team weighed how well each plan worked, how safe each was, and how each shaped drug resistance. Seasonal dosing is cheap and timed to risk, so the best plan matters a lot. Results here guide national plans for child malaria in the whole region. They also warn how fast resistance can blunt a good plan.
plos-pone-0001571:
Matthew Coussens and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a protein and sperm making in mice. The protein, Sirt1, trims tags from other proteins and helps run sugar use, cell survival, and energy work. Its role in male fertility was not set. The team studied mice that lack the protein.

Mice without Sirt1 made far fewer sperm, and their germ cells worked poorly. That ties a broad cell regulator to a sharp fertility role. The finding may bear on male infertility with no clear cause. It also warns that drugs aimed at this protein family must watch fertility effects.
plos-pone-0001671:
Zeena E. Nackerdien, Alexander Keynan, Bonnie L. Bassler, and their co-authors studied how bacteria talk to each other in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Vibrio harveyi is a sea bacterium that glows. Bacteria use quorum sensing, a chemical census, to act as a group once enough of them are present. Because glowing tracks quorum sensing, these bacteria are a favorite system for studying it.

The glow, though, is not a clean marker: glowing itself costs energy and feeds back on growth. The authors measured how quorum sensing changes growth rates in ways the glow marker cannot fully explain. The full text gives the growth curves and the marker checks. The caution matters for the many labs that read bacterial group behavior from light alone.
plos-pone-0001771:
Kamakshi Sureka and co-authors studied how some bacteria in a uniform population survive stress, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Genetically identical microbes behave differently from one another, and that variety lets a subset persist when conditions turn harsh. In mycobacteria, the group that includes the tuberculosis germ, nutrient and oxygen starvation switch on a stress pathway.

The team shows that positive feedback and noise activate Rel, the regulator of the stringent response, in part of the population. The full text gives the single-cell data and the circuit model. A bet-hedging circuit like this helps explain how TB germs can ride out antibiotics and immune attack inside the body.
plos-pone-0001871:
David Gisselsson and co-authors tackled a puzzle about cancer cell division in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In healthy cells, two poles pull the sets of chromosomes apart in a neat, even split. Cancer cells at times divide toward three or more poles at once, which scrambles the sets they pass on.

The team asked how such cells slip past the spindle check, a guard that should halt a flawed split. They also asked how near-random the split of chromosomes then becomes. Their work frames these wild divisions as a source of new gene mixes inside tumors. Readers gain a sharper view of how cancers gain the variety that helps them grow and spread.
plos-pone-0001971:
Sahra Abdulle and co-authors compared HIV subtypes inside the fluid around the brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. HIV-1 comes in many genetic subtypes spread across the world. The virus can enter the brain and spinal fluid, where the immune system reacts in its own closed space.

The team measured viral load in cerebrospinal fluid and signs of immune activation inside the spinal sac, in people infected with unlike subtypes. If subtypes differ in the brain, care and prognosis may need to differ too. The study adds brain data to a field long focused on blood alone.
plos-pone-0002071:
Ajay Wanchu and co-authors tested simple blood markers for tuberculosis in a TB-endemic country, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Spotting TB is harder in people who also carry HIV, and simple biomarkers that work in both groups were needed. Two proteins from the TB bacterium, malate synthase and MPT51, had stood out as strong immune targets in patients.

The team evaluated how sensitive tests for these markers are, in frank TB and in incipient disease, where infection is just taking hold. A cheap marker that catches early cases could change care where TB and HIV overlap most.
plos-pone-0002171:
William Lanier, Ahmed Moustafa, Debashish Bhattacharya, and co-authors read the gene messages of a tiny green alga, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ostreococcus lucimarinus is a pico-eukaryote, a cell with a nucleus barely the size of a bacterium. Its genome, at 13.2 million letters, is among the most compact known in eukaryotes, with genes packed tightly together.

Oddly for so tight a genome, many of its genes still contain introns, the spacer pieces cut out before a gene is used. The team used EST sequences, short reads of active genes, to survey them. They found an excess of introns in the genes the alga uses most.
plos-pone-0002271:
Mark Witton and Darren Naish reappraised the giant flying reptiles called azhdarchid pterosaurs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Azhdarchids were among the most widespread and successful pterosaur groups, with long, shallow beaks and long necks built from stretched, tube-shaped vertebrae. Some stood as tall as giraffes. How they lived and fed, though, stayed controversial.

The authors reviewed the group's functional morphology, what its body plan was built to do, and its paleoecology. They argue against the popular image of these giants skimming water like seabirds. Their reading paints azhdarchids as ground-foraging stalkers of small prey, a very different life for the largest flying animals ever.
plos-pone-0002371:
Polonelli led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Luciano Polonelli, José Pontón, Natalia Elguezabal, among others. Its subject is antibody Complementarity-Determining Regions (CDRs) Can Display Differential Antimicrobial, Antiviral and Antitumor Activities. Complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) are immunoglobulin (Ig) hypervariable domains that determine specific antibody (Ab) binding.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002471:
Scardigli and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Raffaella Scardigli, Cesare Gargioli, Daniela Tosoni, among others. Its subject is binding of sFRP-3 to EGF in the Extra-Cellular Space Affects Proliferation, Differentiation and Morphogenetic Events Regulated by the Two Molecules. sFRP-3 is a soluble antagonist of Wnts, widely expressed in developing embryos.

The Wnt gene family comprises cysteine-rich secreted ligands that regulate cell proliferation, differentiation, organogenesis and oncogenesis of different organisms ranging from worms to mammals. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002571:
Burz joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are David S. Burz, Alexander Shekhtman, among others. Its subject is in-Cell Biochemistry Using NMR Spectroscopy. Biochemistry and structural biology are undergoing a dramatic revolution.

Until now, mostly in vitro techniques have been used to study subtle. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002671:
A 2008 study by Jean Peccoud and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up targeted development of registries of biological parts. The catalog record names Jean Peccoud first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The design and construction of novel biological systems by combining basic building blocks represents a dominant paradigm in synthetic biology. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002771:
Michael C. Otterstatter and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on does pathogen spillover from commercially reared bumble bees threaten wild pollinators?. Authorship is credited in the record to Michael C. Otterstatter and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The conservation of insect pollinators is drawing attention because of reported declines in bee species and the ‘ecosystem services’ they provide. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002871:
Sara E. Heisel, Yuanji Zhang, Edwards Allen and co-authors reported in PLOS ONE in 2008 on small RNAs taken from rice grain. Small RNAs are short molecules, about 20 to 24 units long, that help guide growth in plants and animals. The team compared RNA from mature grain with RNA from young seedlings.

To map the groups they used pyrosequencing, a fast DNA reading method, plus a clustering program to find where the RNAs sit in the genome. The paper describes which small RNA groups appear unique to grain. Plant scientists can use that map to study how rice seeds form and store food.
plos-pone-0002971:
Yone Jung Yoon, Hisashi Kominami, Thomas Trimarchi and co-authors blocked electrical activity in the chick spinal cord in 2008. Spontaneous activity in the cord's networks guides how neurons specialize and how nerve-muscle structures are built during development. The team examined what chronic loss of that activity does.

They used retroviral infection to add Kir2.1 channels, which quiet electrical activity, to developing cells. That disrupted the electrical differentiation of motoneurons, the nerve cells that drive muscles. Published in PLOS ONE, the study shows activity is not a by-product but a teacher in spinal development. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003071:
Satsuki Fukushima, Steven Coppen, Joon Lee and co-authors compared delivery routes for myoblast therapy in rat heart failure in 2008. Injecting skeletal myoblasts into heart muscle had shown promise for post-infarction chronic heart failure. Weak benefit and ventricular arrhythmias were the standing concerns.

The team tested choice of cell-delivery route for the transplant. Route decides how many cells stay in the heart and where they lodge. Published in PLOS ONE, delivery is often the difference between a therapy that works in principle and one that works in practice, making this comparison valuable. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003171:
Yongping Wang, Yun E. Wang, M. Grazia Cotticelli and colleagues describe a new RNA interference library in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. RNA interference blocks gene activity through small non-coding RNAs. Most libraries target single genes through standard pathways. The body's own microRNAs, however, often target many genes at once and can act through other routes.

The authors build a random shRNA-encoding library for phenotypic selection and hit optimization. Readers get a tool that searches by outcome first, then finds the active sequences. Such screens can reveal gene effects that one-by-one testing would miss, including effects spread across several targets.
plos-pone-0003271:
Tiziana Musso, Sara Scutera, William Vermi and colleagues study a signal that makes Langerhans cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Langerhans cells are a well characterized subset of dendritic cells located in the epidermis of skin and mucosae. In the body they originate from resident and blood-borne precursors in the presence of keratinocyte-derived TGF-beta. In vitro, they can be generated from monocytes.

The title reports that activin A induces Langerhans cell differentiation in vitro and in human skin explants. Readers get another route to produce a key skin immune cell. Lab-grown Langerhans cells help study allergy, infection, and skin immune responses.
plos-pone-0007471: GLI3 is a transcription factor steered by the Sonic Hedgehog signal, and single-letter mutations in it cause birth-defect syndromes like Greig cephalopolysyndactyly.
